questiontext.text: What is Acceptance Test-Driven Development (ATDD)?

answer.text: A collaborative practice in which the team agrees on acceptance tests for a requirement, written from the customer's perspective, before the feature is developed

feedback.text: Correct — ATDD agrees acceptance tests up front, collaboratively, and drives development from them.

answer.text: A way for testers to write bug reports after the developers have finished coding a feature

feedback.text: ATDD is test-first and collaborative; it is not after-the-fact bug reporting by testers alone.

answer.text: A profiling technique for measuring how long each acceptance test takes to run

feedback.text: That is performance measurement; ATDD is about agreeing acceptance tests before development.

answer.text: A tool that automatically generates production code from a database schema

feedback.text: ATDD is a collaboration and specification practice, not a code generator.

generalfeedback.text: ATDD (Acceptance Test-Driven Development) has the whole team — business, developers, and testers — agree on concrete acceptance tests for a requirement before it is built. Those tests are written from the customer/business perspective, express what "done" means, and drive the implementation outside-in.

questiontext.text: What is an acceptance test in ATDD?

answer.text: A test, expressed from the customer/business point of view, that checks whether a feature satisfies an agreed requirement

feedback.text: Correct — an acceptance test verifies the feature against the customer's expectation of the requirement.

answer.text: A test that a single developer writes to check one small internal function in isolation

feedback.text: That describes a unit test; an acceptance test works at the customer/requirement level.

answer.text: A measurement of how much of the source code the test suite executes

feedback.text: That is code coverage; an acceptance test verifies a requirement from the customer's view.

answer.text: A checklist of coding-style rules the code must follow

feedback.text: Style rules are a linting concern; an acceptance test checks customer-facing behaviour.

generalfeedback.text: An acceptance test states, in customer/business terms, what the feature must do to be accepted. Unlike a developer unit test (which checks internal units), it captures the requirement as the customer sees it and is the yardstick for whether the feature is "done".

questiontext.text: The commonly taught ATDD cycle has four stages. What are their names?

answer.text: Discuss, Distill, Develop, Demo

feedback.text: Correct — the four stages of the ATDD cycle are Discuss, Distill, Develop, and Demo.

answer.text: Red, Green, Refactor, Release

feedback.text: Red-Green-Refactor is the TDD micro-cycle, not the four-stage ATDD cycle.

answer.text: Plan, Do, Check, Act

feedback.text: That is the PDCA improvement cycle; the ATDD cycle is Discuss, Distill, Develop, Demo.

answer.text: Design, Deploy, Debug, Document

feedback.text: Those are not the ATDD stages; the four are Discuss, Distill, Develop, Demo.

generalfeedback.text: Markus Gärtner's widely taught ATDD cycle has four stages: Discuss (talk through a requirement with examples), Distill (turn examples into acceptance tests), Develop (implement and make the tests pass), and Demo (show/verify the feature with stakeholders).

questiontext.text: In the ATDD cycle, what happens in the Discuss stage?

answer.text: The team talks through the requirement or story with stakeholders, using concrete examples to build a shared understanding

feedback.text: Correct — Discuss explores the requirement with stakeholders through concrete examples.

answer.text: The team writes the production code that implements the feature

feedback.text: Implementation happens in Develop; Discuss is the conversation about the requirement.

answer.text: The team shows the finished feature to the product owner for sign-off

feedback.text: That is Demo; Discuss comes first and is about understanding the requirement.

answer.text: The team measures branch coverage of the acceptance suite

feedback.text: Coverage measurement is unrelated; Discuss is the shared conversation using examples.

generalfeedback.text: Discuss is the first stage: the team and stakeholders talk through a user story or requirement, raising concrete examples and edge cases so everyone shares the same understanding of what is wanted before any test is written or code is built.

questiontext.text: In the ATDD cycle, what happens in the Distill stage?

answer.text: The concrete examples from the discussion are turned into acceptance tests / acceptance criteria, often in Given-When-Then form

feedback.text: Correct — Distill converts the agreed examples into acceptance tests.

answer.text: The team deploys the release to the production servers

feedback.text: Deployment is not an ATDD stage; Distill turns examples into acceptance tests.

answer.text: The team brainstorms the requirement with the customer for the first time

feedback.text: That first conversation is Discuss; Distill formalises its examples into tests.

answer.text: The team profiles the feature to find performance bottlenecks

feedback.text: Profiling is unrelated; Distill produces the acceptance tests from the examples.

generalfeedback.text: Distill is the second stage: the examples raised while discussing are refined and written down as acceptance tests (acceptance criteria), frequently in a Given-When-Then structure. These become the shared, agreed definition of what the feature must do.

questiontext.text: In the ATDD cycle, what happens in the Develop stage?

answer.text: Developers implement the feature and make the acceptance test pass, typically using unit-level TDD (red-green-refactor) inside

feedback.text: Correct — Develop builds the feature to satisfy the acceptance test, using TDD internally.

answer.text: The team only talks about the requirement and writes nothing

feedback.text: Talking is Discuss; Develop is where the feature is actually implemented.

answer.text: The team deletes the acceptance tests so they do not slow the build

feedback.text: Acceptance tests are kept and made to pass; they are not deleted in Develop.

answer.text: The customer signs off on the finished feature

feedback.text: Sign-off happens in Demo; Develop is the implementation stage.

generalfeedback.text: Develop is the third stage: developers write the code that makes the agreed acceptance test pass. Inside this stage they normally use ordinary unit-level TDD (red-green-refactor), so ATDD's acceptance-level loop wraps around the developer's unit-level loop.

questiontext.text: In the ATDD cycle, what happens in the Demo stage?

answer.text: The finished feature is shown to and verified with stakeholders to confirm it meets the agreed acceptance criteria

feedback.text: Correct — Demo verifies with stakeholders that the feature satisfies the acceptance criteria.

answer.text: The team first discovers what the requirement is

feedback.text: Discovering the requirement is Discuss; Demo confirms the finished result.

answer.text: The team writes the acceptance tests from examples

feedback.text: Writing the tests is Distill; Demo shows the completed feature against them.

answer.text: The team refactors internal code with no stakeholder present

feedback.text: Refactoring is part of Develop; Demo is the stakeholder verification.

generalfeedback.text: Demo is the fourth stage: the completed feature is demonstrated to stakeholders and checked against the acceptance criteria agreed earlier. It closes the loop by confirming, with the people who asked for it, that the right thing was built.

questiontext.text: In ATDD, who are the Three Amigos?

answer.text: A business/product representative, a developer, and a tester, who together specify the acceptance criteria

feedback.text: Correct — the three perspectives are business/PO, developer, and tester.

answer.text: Three senior developers who review each other's code

feedback.text: The Three Amigos are three different roles (business, dev, tester), not three developers.

answer.text: The project manager, the scrum master, and the release manager

feedback.text: The Three Amigos are the business/PO, a developer, and a tester — not management roles.

answer.text: Three separate automated testing tools

feedback.text: The Three Amigos are people bringing three perspectives, not tools.

generalfeedback.text: The "Three Amigos" are three viewpoints brought together to specify acceptance criteria: the business/product owner (what and why), the developer (how it can be built), and the tester (how it could fail or be misunderstood). Their collaboration is central to ATDD.

questiontext.text: What does Specification by Example mean?

answer.text: Requirements are captured as concrete, agreed examples that become executable specifications and living documentation

feedback.text: Correct — concrete examples serve as the specification and can be run to verify the system.

answer.text: Requirements are written only as abstract prose with no examples

feedback.text: The opposite — the whole point is to use concrete examples rather than vague prose.

answer.text: Examples are used to illustrate a document but can never be executed

feedback.text: In Specification by Example the examples become executable, not merely illustrative.

answer.text: Production code is written first and examples are added afterwards

feedback.text: Examples are agreed before/with development and drive it; they are not an afterthought.

generalfeedback.text: Specification by Example (closely related to ATDD) captures requirements as concrete, agreed examples. Backed by automation, those examples run as acceptance tests, so they specify the behaviour and simultaneously verify it — and they stay accurate as living documentation.

name.text: Acceptance tests are written before development

questiontext.text: In ATDD, the acceptance tests for a feature are agreed and written before that feature is developed.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — ATDD is test-first at the acceptance level: the tests come before development.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: ATDD is test-first: acceptance tests are agreed before the feature is built, not after.

generalfeedback.text: The "Test-Driven" in Acceptance Test-Driven Development means the acceptance tests are written first. Agreeing them before development gives the team a shared target and a definition of "done" that drives the implementation.

questiontext.text: Which statement best describes who is involved in ATDD?

answer.text: It is a collaborative activity in which business, developers, and testers together specify the acceptance tests

feedback.text: Correct — ATDD is a whole-team collaboration, not the work of one role.

answer.text: It is done solely by testers, working alone after the code is written

feedback.text: ATDD is collaborative and test-first; it is not a solo, after-coding tester activity.

answer.text: It is done solely by developers, with no business or tester input

feedback.text: Business and testers are essential; ATDD needs all three perspectives.

answer.text: It is done solely by the product owner, who hands finished tests to the team

feedback.text: The tests are produced together; the PO does not write them alone.

generalfeedback.text: A defining feature of ATDD is collaboration: the business/product owner, developers, and testers jointly agree the acceptance tests. This shared authorship is what creates a single, common understanding of "done".

questiontext.text: In ATDD, what do the agreed acceptance criteria primarily establish?

answer.text: A shared definition of "done" — the conditions the feature must satisfy to be accepted

feedback.text: Correct — acceptance criteria are the agreed definition of when the feature is done.

answer.text: The exact number of unit tests each class must have

feedback.text: That is a code-metric target; acceptance criteria define what the feature must do to be accepted.

answer.text: The deployment schedule for the release

feedback.text: Scheduling is a planning concern; acceptance criteria define "done" for the feature.

answer.text: The coding style the team must follow

feedback.text: Style is a separate concern; acceptance criteria capture the required behaviour.

generalfeedback.text: Acceptance criteria, agreed by the team, state what a feature must do to be accepted by the customer. They form the shared definition of "done", turning a vague requirement into a concrete, checkable target.

questiontext.text: Acceptance criteria in ATDD are often written in a Given-When-Then form. What do those three parts express?

answer.text: A precondition (Given), an action or event (When), and the expected outcome (Then)

feedback.text: Correct — Given-When-Then captures context, action, and expected result.

answer.text: Three developers who must approve the test

feedback.text: Given-When-Then is a structure for one example, not a list of approvers.

answer.text: The three environments dev, staging, and production

feedback.text: Given-When-Then describes context/action/outcome, not environments.

answer.text: The past, present, and future versions of the feature

feedback.text: They are the parts of one acceptance example: precondition, action, outcome.

generalfeedback.text: Given-When-Then is a common way to phrase an acceptance test or criterion: Given a starting context, When an action occurs, Then an observable outcome should hold. It makes a concrete example precise enough to be automated.

questiontext.text: ATDD is often described as an outside-in approach. What does that mean?

answer.text: Development is driven from the outside — the customer-facing acceptance criteria — inward to the implementation

feedback.text: Correct — ATDD starts from customer-level acceptance tests and works inward to the code.

answer.text: Development starts from the database schema and works outward to the UI

feedback.text: That is an inside-out, data-first approach; ATDD drives from customer criteria inward.

answer.text: Testing is performed only by people outside the company

feedback.text: "Outside-in" refers to starting from customer requirements, not to outsourcing testing.

answer.text: Code is written first and requirements are inferred afterwards

feedback.text: ATDD agrees the customer-level requirement first, then builds inward to satisfy it.

generalfeedback.text: Outside-in means you begin at the boundary the customer cares about — the acceptance criteria — and let those drive the design of the internals. ATDD's acceptance tests set the target, and the implementation is grown inward to satisfy them.

questiontext.text: The acronym ATDD stands for "Acceptance Test-Driven Development".

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — ATDD expands to Acceptance Test-Driven Development.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: ATDD does stand for Acceptance Test-Driven Development.

generalfeedback.text: ATDD = Acceptance Test-Driven Development: development driven by acceptance tests that are agreed, from the customer's perspective, before the feature is built.

questiontext.text: What is the correct order of the four ATDD cycle stages?

answer.text: Discuss, then Distill, then Develop, then Demo

feedback.text: Correct — understand the requirement, capture it as tests, build it, then verify with stakeholders.

answer.text: Distill, then Discuss, then Demo, then Develop

feedback.text: You must Discuss before you can Distill examples, and Develop before you Demo.

answer.text: Develop, then Discuss, then Distill, then Demo

feedback.text: Building before discussing and distilling defeats the purpose; Discuss comes first.

answer.text: Demo, then Develop, then Distill, then Discuss

feedback.text: That is fully reversed; the cycle runs Discuss, Distill, Develop, Demo.

generalfeedback.text: The ATDD cycle flows Discuss (understand the requirement with examples), Distill (turn examples into acceptance tests), Develop (implement and make them pass), Demo (verify with stakeholders). Each stage feeds the next.

questiontext.text: During Distill, what is the main output the team produces?

answer.text: Acceptance tests / acceptance criteria (often Given-When-Then) derived from the agreed examples

feedback.text: Correct — Distill converts the discussion's examples into concrete acceptance tests.

answer.text: The production implementation of the feature

feedback.text: Implementation is the Develop output; Distill produces the acceptance tests.

answer.text: A stakeholder sign-off that the feature is finished

feedback.text: Sign-off comes in Demo; Distill produces the tests that Demo later checks against.

answer.text: A performance benchmark report

feedback.text: Benchmarking is unrelated; Distill yields the acceptance criteria.

generalfeedback.text: Distill takes the concrete examples raised in Discuss and refines them into precise acceptance tests / criteria — frequently written as Given-When-Then. These agreed tests are the target the Develop stage will implement against.

questiontext.text: What distinguishes the Demo stage from the others?

answer.text: It brings the stakeholders back to verify that the finished feature meets the acceptance criteria agreed earlier

feedback.text: Correct — Demo is the stakeholder verification that the right thing was built.

answer.text: It is where developers first learn what the requirement is

feedback.text: Requirements are understood in Discuss; Demo confirms the completed feature.

answer.text: It is where the acceptance tests are first written from examples

feedback.text: Writing the tests is Distill; Demo checks the built feature against them.

answer.text: It is where developers refactor internal code without any stakeholder

feedback.text: Refactoring happens in Develop; Demo is explicitly a stakeholder verification.

generalfeedback.text: Demo closes the loop with the people who asked for the feature. The team shows the completed work and checks it against the acceptance criteria distilled earlier, confirming — with stakeholders present — that it satisfies the requirement.

questiontext.text: Why does ATDD bring together three roles (the Three Amigos) to specify acceptance criteria?

answer.text: Because business, developer, and tester each notice different things — value and intent, feasibility, and ways it could fail — so together they specify more complete, correct criteria

feedback.text: Correct — the three viewpoints complement each other and catch gaps a single role would miss.

answer.text: Because three signatures are legally required before coding may start

feedback.text: It is about complementary perspectives, not a legal sign-off requirement.

answer.text: Because it lets the work be split so no one has to talk to anyone else

feedback.text: The point is collaboration and conversation, not avoiding it.

answer.text: Because three people always write code faster than one

feedback.text: The Three Amigos meet to specify criteria, not to speed up typing code.

generalfeedback.text: Each amigo brings a distinct lens: the business/PO clarifies what is wanted and why, the developer flags what is feasible and any hidden complexity, and the tester probes edge cases and ambiguity. Combining the three yields acceptance criteria that are clearer and less likely to miss something.

questiontext.text: What is the key difference between ATDD and ordinary TDD?

answer.text: ATDD drives development from customer-facing acceptance tests agreed with the business, while TDD drives it from developer-written unit tests at the code level

feedback.text: Correct — ATDD works at the acceptance/customer level; TDD at the unit/developer level.

answer.text: ATDD writes tests after the code, while TDD writes them before

feedback.text: Both are test-first; the difference is the level (acceptance/customer vs unit/developer).

answer.text: ATDD is only manual testing, while TDD is only automated

feedback.text: Both can be automated; the real distinction is acceptance level versus unit level.

answer.text: ATDD forbids unit tests, while TDD forbids acceptance tests

feedback.text: They coexist: ATDD's Develop stage typically uses unit-level TDD inside.

generalfeedback.text: Both ATDD and TDD are test-first. TDD operates at the unit level — a developer writes a failing unit test, makes it pass, then refactors (red-green-refactor). ATDD operates at the acceptance level — the team agrees customer-facing acceptance tests that drive the feature outside-in. In practice, ATDD's Develop stage uses TDD inside.

questiontext.text: How is BDD related to ATDD?

answer.text: They are closely related, example-driven, collaborative practices; BDD especially emphasises describing behaviour in a shared, ubiquitous language (e.g. Gherkin's Given-When-Then)

feedback.text: Correct — BDD is a close relative of ATDD with a strong emphasis on behaviour and shared language.

answer.text: BDD is a performance-testing technique unrelated to ATDD

feedback.text: BDD is about specifying behaviour by example, closely aligned with ATDD, not performance.

answer.text: BDD writes tests only after release, the opposite of ATDD

feedback.text: BDD, like ATDD, favours specifying behaviour before/with development.

answer.text: BDD replaces all collaboration with fully automated code generation

feedback.text: BDD is a collaboration and specification practice, not code generation.

generalfeedback.text: BDD and ATDD overlap heavily: both are collaborative and example-driven, and both specify behaviour before development. BDD puts particular emphasis on describing behaviour in a ubiquitous language shared by the whole team, often using Gherkin (Given-When-Then). Many teams treat their ATDD acceptance tests as BDD scenarios.

questiontext.text: While making an acceptance test pass in the Develop stage, what do developers typically do at the code level?

answer.text: Use unit-level TDD (red-green-refactor) to grow the implementation until the acceptance test passes

feedback.text: Correct — the acceptance loop wraps around an inner unit-level TDD loop.

answer.text: Skip all unit tests because the acceptance test already exists

feedback.text: Unit tests are not skipped; TDD is normally used inside Develop.

answer.text: Rewrite the acceptance criteria to match whatever code they produce

feedback.text: The agreed criteria are the target; you build to them, not rewrite them to fit the code.

answer.text: Wait for the Demo stage to write any tests at all

feedback.text: Tests are written before and during development, not deferred to Demo.

generalfeedback.text: ATDD nests loops: the outer loop is the acceptance test agreed with the business, and inside Develop the developer typically uses ordinary unit-level TDD (red-green-refactor) to build the code that eventually makes the acceptance test pass. Acceptance and unit tests complement each other.

questiontext.text: What makes the Discuss conversation effective in ATDD?

answer.text: Grounding the requirement in concrete examples so ambiguity surfaces and everyone shares the same understanding

feedback.text: Correct — concrete examples expose misunderstandings early and align the team.

answer.text: Keeping the requirement as abstract as possible so it stays flexible

feedback.text: Abstraction hides ambiguity; concrete examples are what make Discuss effective.

answer.text: Having only the developer present so decisions are quick

feedback.text: Discuss needs the stakeholders' input, not just a developer.

answer.text: Writing the production code during the meeting

feedback.text: Coding is Develop; Discuss is about understanding via examples.

generalfeedback.text: Discuss works best when the team explores the requirement through concrete examples ("what should happen if...?"). Real cases and edge cases quickly reveal hidden assumptions and disagreements, producing a genuinely shared understanding before any test or code is written.

questiontext.text: Which stage of the ATDD cycle comes first?

answer.text: Discuss

feedback.text: Correct — the cycle begins by discussing the requirement with stakeholders.

answer.text: Develop

feedback.text: Develop is third; the cycle starts with Discuss.

answer.text: Demo

feedback.text: Demo is last; the cycle starts with Discuss.

answer.text: Distill

feedback.text: Distill is second; it follows the Discuss conversation.

generalfeedback.text: The cycle opens with Discuss: understanding the requirement with stakeholders through examples. Only then can the team Distill those examples into acceptance tests, Develop the feature, and Demo it.

questiontext.text: Which stage of the ATDD cycle comes last?

answer.text: Demo

feedback.text: Correct — the cycle ends by demonstrating and verifying the feature with stakeholders.

answer.text: Distill

feedback.text: Distill is second; the cycle ends with Demo.

answer.text: Discuss

feedback.text: Discuss is first; the cycle ends with Demo.

answer.text: Develop

feedback.text: Develop is third; Demo follows it as the final stage.

generalfeedback.text: Demo is the final stage: after Discuss, Distill, and Develop, the team shows the finished feature to stakeholders and verifies it against the agreed acceptance criteria.

questiontext.text: In what sense do acceptance tests "drive" development in ATDD?

answer.text: They are agreed first and act as the target the implementation must satisfy, guiding what gets built and defining when it is done

feedback.text: Correct — the agreed acceptance tests set the goal that development works toward.

answer.text: They are generated automatically from the finished code

feedback.text: Acceptance tests are agreed before development, not generated from finished code.

answer.text: They are used only to reject the work at the very end

feedback.text: They guide the work throughout, not merely as a final gate.

answer.text: They replace any need to talk to the customer

feedback.text: They come from customer collaboration; they do not replace it.

generalfeedback.text: Because the acceptance tests are agreed before coding and express what "done" means, they set the target for the whole effort. Development proceeds until those tests pass, so the tests shape and drive what gets built rather than merely judging it afterwards.

questiontext.text: In a Three Amigos conversation, what does the business/product representative mainly contribute?

answer.text: Clarity about what is wanted and why — the business value and intent behind the requirement

feedback.text: Correct — the business voice defines the desired outcome and its value.

answer.text: The unit-test structure the developers should use internally

feedback.text: Internal test structure is the developer's area, not the business representative's.

answer.text: The exact edge cases and failure modes to probe

feedback.text: Probing edge cases is chiefly the tester's contribution; business supplies intent and value.

answer.text: The continuous-integration pipeline configuration

feedback.text: CI setup is not the business representative's role in the conversation.

generalfeedback.text: The business/product owner brings the "what and why": the outcome the customer needs and the value behind it. The developer weighs feasibility and the tester probes how it could go wrong. Together the three specify well-rounded acceptance criteria.

questiontext.text: In a Three Amigos conversation, what does the tester mainly contribute?

answer.text: Questions about edge cases, ambiguity, and how the feature could fail or be misunderstood

feedback.text: Correct — the tester probes for gaps, edge cases, and ways the requirement could break.

answer.text: The final business decision on whether the feature is worth building

feedback.text: That call belongs to the business/PO; the tester probes correctness and completeness.

answer.text: The choice of programming language and frameworks

feedback.text: Technical implementation choices are the developer's area, not the tester's core role here.

answer.text: Nothing — the tester only writes tests after coding is finished

feedback.text: In ATDD the tester participates up front in specifying criteria, not only afterwards.

generalfeedback.text: The tester's lens is "how could this be wrong or misunderstood?" — surfacing edge cases, ambiguities, and failure modes while the criteria are still being written. This up-front questioning is far cheaper than discovering the gaps after the feature is built.

questiontext.text: Why can ATDD/Specification-by-Example acceptance tests serve as living documentation?

answer.text: Because they are executed against the system, a passing suite shows the documented examples still match the real behaviour, so the documentation cannot silently go stale

feedback.text: Correct — executing the examples keeps the documentation in step with the system.

answer.text: Because they are printed and stored in a binder for reference

feedback.text: Living documentation is executable and self-checking, not a static archive.

answer.text: Because a writer manually rewrites them after every release

feedback.text: The point is that execution keeps them current automatically, not manual rewriting.

answer.text: Because they can be read but never run

feedback.text: They are run against the system; that is exactly what keeps them alive.

generalfeedback.text: Ordinary documents drift from the code over time. Because ATDD acceptance tests (concrete examples) are executed, any behaviour change that is not reflected in them makes them fail. A green suite is evidence the examples still describe the real system — documentation that stays alive.

name.text: ATDD versus TDD: wrong thing versus wrong code

questiontext.text: At the level each works, what kind of mistake does ATDD most directly guard against compared with TDD?

answer.text: ATDD mainly guards against building the wrong thing (wrong requirement), while TDD mainly guards against building the thing wrong (defective code)

feedback.text: Correct — acceptance-level ATDD targets requirement correctness; unit-level TDD targets code correctness.

answer.text: ATDD guards against slow code, while TDD guards against slow tests

feedback.text: Neither is about speed; ATDD targets the right requirement, TDD targets correct code.

answer.text: They guard against exactly the same mistakes at the same level

feedback.text: They work at different levels: acceptance/customer versus unit/developer.

answer.text: ATDD guards against compiler errors, while TDD guards against typos

feedback.text: That trivialises both; ATDD is about the right requirement, TDD about correct units.

generalfeedback.text: Because ATDD agrees customer-facing acceptance tests first, it chiefly protects against building the wrong feature — a requirement mismatch. TDD, working at the unit level, chiefly protects against defects in the code that is built. The two levels are complementary: right thing (ATDD) and thing done right (TDD).

name.text: Place activity: turning examples into Given-When-Then

questiontext.text: The team takes the concrete examples agreed in a story conversation and writes them up as Given-When-Then acceptance tests. Which ATDD stage is this?

answer.text: Distill

feedback.text: Correct — converting agreed examples into acceptance tests is the Distill stage.

answer.text: Discuss

feedback.text: Discuss is the conversation that surfaces the examples; writing them up as tests is Distill.

answer.text: Develop

feedback.text: Develop implements the feature; formalising examples into tests is Distill.

answer.text: Demo

feedback.text: Demo verifies the finished feature; producing the acceptance tests is Distill.

generalfeedback.text: Distill is exactly this: taking the concrete examples raised while discussing and refining them into precise acceptance tests, often as Given-When-Then. The output is the agreed criteria the Develop stage will build toward.

name.text: Place activity: showing the feature to the PO

questiontext.text: The developers show the completed feature to the product owner and walk through the acceptance criteria together to confirm it is right. Which ATDD stage is this?

answer.text: Demo

feedback.text: Correct — verifying the finished feature with stakeholders is the Demo stage.

answer.text: Discuss

feedback.text: Discuss happens before building; confirming the finished feature is Demo.

answer.text: Distill

feedback.text: Distill produces the acceptance tests; checking the built feature against them is Demo.

answer.text: Develop

feedback.text: Develop is the implementation; the stakeholder verification afterwards is Demo.

generalfeedback.text: Demonstrating the completed work to stakeholders and confirming, with them, that it satisfies the agreed acceptance criteria is the Demo stage — the point where the team verifies it built the right thing.

questiontext.text: A developer writes a failing unit test, makes it pass, and refactors, repeating this while building the code that will satisfy the acceptance test. Which ATDD stage does this happen in?

answer.text: Develop — unit-level TDD is used inside the Develop stage

feedback.text: Correct — red-green-refactor is the inner TDD loop within Develop.

answer.text: Distill — because that is where all tests are written

feedback.text: Distill writes the acceptance tests; unit-level red-green-refactor happens in Develop.

answer.text: Discuss — because coding starts as soon as the conversation begins

feedback.text: Discuss is conversation; the coding with unit TDD is the Develop stage.

answer.text: Demo — because tests are run in front of stakeholders

feedback.text: Demo verifies the finished feature; the red-green-refactor coding is in Develop.

generalfeedback.text: Inside Develop, the team makes the acceptance test pass by growing the implementation with ordinary unit-level TDD (red-green-refactor). ATDD's acceptance loop wraps around this inner unit-test loop; the two operate at different levels.

questiontext.text: What is the strongest reason to agree the acceptance tests before starting development?

answer.text: It builds a shared understanding of "done" up front, reducing the risk of building the wrong thing and giving a clear target

feedback.text: Correct — agreeing tests first aligns everyone and prevents wasted effort on the wrong feature.

answer.text: It guarantees the code will contain no bugs whatsoever

feedback.text: No practice guarantees zero bugs; ATDD's value is shared understanding and a clear target.

answer.text: It lets the team skip talking to the customer later

feedback.text: ATDD is built on ongoing collaboration; it does not remove the need to communicate.

answer.text: It makes unit tests unnecessary

feedback.text: Unit tests still matter; ATDD's Develop stage typically uses TDD inside.

generalfeedback.text: Agreeing acceptance tests up front forces the business, developers, and testers to reach one concrete definition of "done" before effort is spent. That shared understanding is the main defence against the costliest failure — building the wrong thing well.

name.text: Misconception: ATDD is only a tester activity

questiontext.text: A colleague says, "ATDD is just the testers' job — they write the acceptance tests and hand them over." Why is this wrong?

answer.text: ATDD is collaborative: business, developers, and testers specify the acceptance tests together, so it is a whole-team activity, not a tester-only one

feedback.text: Correct — the Three Amigos collaboration is central; ATDD is not owned by testers alone.

answer.text: It is wrong because only developers are allowed to write acceptance tests

feedback.text: No single role owns it; the point is that all three collaborate, testers included.

answer.text: It is correct — testers do own ATDD entirely

feedback.text: That is the misconception; ATDD is a collaborative, whole-team practice.

answer.text: It is wrong because ATDD does not involve tests at all

feedback.text: ATDD is very much about acceptance tests; the error is thinking only testers make them.

generalfeedback.text: A core idea of ATDD is shared authorship of the acceptance criteria. The Three Amigos — business/PO, developer, tester — specify them together so the whole team owns one definition of "done". Treating it as a testers-only handoff loses the shared understanding that gives ATDD its value.

questiontext.text: A team writes the code first and only then writes acceptance tests to check it. Why is this not ATDD?

answer.text: ATDD is test-first at the acceptance level: the tests must be agreed before development so they can drive it and define "done"

feedback.text: Correct — writing acceptance tests after the code inverts the "test-driven" idea of ATDD.

answer.text: It is not ATDD because acceptance tests may never be automated

feedback.text: Automation is not the issue; the issue is that the tests came after the code, not before.

answer.text: It is actually correct ATDD, since the order does not matter

feedback.text: Order is central: ATDD requires the acceptance tests to come before development.

answer.text: It is not ATDD because ATDD forbids writing any code

feedback.text: ATDD includes a Develop stage; the point is the tests precede that development.

generalfeedback.text: The "Test-Driven" in ATDD means the acceptance tests come first and shape what gets built. Writing them after the fact turns them into a verification checklist and forfeits the shared, up-front definition of "done" that drives the work.

questiontext.text: "Because ATDD already has an acceptance test, the Develop stage doesn't need any unit testing." Why is this a misconception?

answer.text: The Develop stage normally uses unit-level TDD inside; acceptance and unit tests operate at different levels and complement each other

feedback.text: Correct — the acceptance loop wraps an inner unit-level TDD loop; both are used.

answer.text: It is correct — one acceptance test fully replaces all unit tests

feedback.text: An acceptance test checks customer-level behaviour; it does not replace fine-grained unit tests.

answer.text: It is a misconception because acceptance tests cannot be automated

feedback.text: Acceptance tests can be automated; the error is thinking they remove the need for unit tests.

answer.text: It is a misconception because Develop is where acceptance tests are first written

feedback.text: Acceptance tests are written in Distill; the error here is dropping unit testing in Develop.

generalfeedback.text: ATDD nests loops. The outer, acceptance-level test defines customer-facing "done"; inside Develop, developers still use unit-level TDD (red-green-refactor) to build and verify the internals. The two levels catch different problems and are used together, not one instead of the other.

questiontext.text: Consider two tests for a checkout feature. Test X, agreed with the product owner, says "Given a cart of $100 with a 10% coupon, When the customer checks out, Then the total is $90." Test Y, written by a developer, checks that the internal applyDiscount() function returns 90 for inputs (100, 0.10). Which is the ATDD-style acceptance test?

answer.text: Test X — it is customer-facing, agreed with the business, and expressed as observable behaviour

feedback.text: Correct — X is an acceptance test; Y is a developer unit test.

answer.text: Test Y — because it uses concrete numbers

feedback.text: Both use numbers; Y checks an internal function, so it is a unit test, not an acceptance test.

answer.text: Both are unit tests, since both involve a discount

feedback.text: X is agreed with the business and describes customer behaviour — that is an acceptance test.

answer.text: Neither is a test because no code is shown

feedback.text: Both are tests; X is the acceptance-level one and Y is the unit-level one.

generalfeedback.text: Test X describes end-to-end, customer-visible behaviour agreed with the business — an ATDD acceptance test. Test Y verifies one internal function in isolation — a developer unit test (TDD). Both are valuable and typically coexist: Y is the kind of test written inside Develop to help make X pass.

questiontext.text: Two teams both agree acceptance tests before coding. Team A writes them as ad-hoc checklists; Team B writes them as Given-When-Then scenarios in a ubiquitous language shared with the business and runs them with a Cucumber-style tool. Which best describes Team B's emphasis?

answer.text: It reflects the BDD emphasis: describing behaviour in a shared, ubiquitous language (Gherkin's Given-When-Then) that both people and tools can read

feedback.text: Correct — Team B leans into BDD's focus on behaviour and shared language, a close relative of ATDD.

answer.text: It shows Team B is doing unit-level TDD rather than acceptance testing

feedback.text: Given-When-Then scenarios are acceptance-level behaviour, not unit-level TDD.

answer.text: It shows Team B has abandoned collaboration with the business

feedback.text: The opposite — a ubiquitous language shared with the business strengthens collaboration.

answer.text: It shows Team B is doing performance testing

feedback.text: Given-When-Then scenarios describe functional behaviour, not performance.

generalfeedback.text: Both teams practise ATDD (acceptance tests first, collaboratively). Team B additionally embraces BDD's emphasis: expressing behaviour in a ubiquitous language via Gherkin (Given-When-Then) and executing it with tools like Cucumber. BDD is a close relative of ATDD that foregrounds shared language and behaviour.

questiontext.text: Throughout the ATDD cycle, why are concrete examples (Specification by Example) so important?

answer.text: They pin down ambiguous requirements precisely, become the executable acceptance tests, and double as living documentation of real behaviour

feedback.text: Correct — concrete examples align understanding, drive the tests, and stay accurate as documentation.

answer.text: They exist only to make meetings longer and are discarded before coding

feedback.text: Examples are kept and turned into the acceptance tests; they are not thrown away.

answer.text: They replace the need for any conversation between roles

feedback.text: Examples are the product of conversation, not a substitute for it.

answer.text: They are only useful for measuring code coverage

feedback.text: Their role is shared understanding and executable specification, not coverage measurement.

generalfeedback.text: Concrete examples make a fuzzy requirement precise ("what exactly should happen when...?"). Distilled into acceptance tests, they specify the behaviour, verify it when run, and remain trustworthy documentation of what the system actually does — the essence of Specification by Example.

name.text: Cost of a missing amigo perspective

questiontext.text: A team specifies acceptance criteria with only the product owner and a developer present; no tester takes part. What is the most likely consequence?

answer.text: Edge cases, ambiguities, and failure modes are more likely to be missed, so the criteria are less complete and gaps surface later

feedback.text: Correct — without the tester's lens, exactly the "how could this go wrong?" cases tend to slip through.

answer.text: The criteria will be perfect, since two roles are enough for any requirement

feedback.text: Missing the tester's perspective typically leaves edge cases and ambiguities unaddressed.

answer.text: Development will be impossible to start without a tester's signature

feedback.text: It is not about a signature; it is about the missing viewpoint reducing the quality of the criteria.

answer.text: The feature will automatically have full unit-test coverage

feedback.text: The Three Amigos concerns specifying criteria, not generating unit-test coverage.

generalfeedback.text: Each amigo covers a blind spot of the others. The tester specifically probes edge cases, ambiguity, and failure modes. Leaving that lens out of the conversation means such gaps are less likely to be caught early, and they tend to reappear as defects or rework once the feature is built.

name.text: Order a full set of activities

questiontext.text: Put these four activities into the correct ATDD order: (1) implement the feature with unit TDD until the acceptance test passes; (2) show the finished feature to stakeholders for verification; (3) talk through the story with concrete examples; (4) write the examples up as acceptance tests.

answer.text: 3, then 4, then 1, then 2

feedback.text: Correct — Discuss (3), Distill (4), Develop (1), Demo (2).

answer.text: 4, then 3, then 2, then 1

feedback.text: You discuss before distilling, and develop before demoing; this order is wrong.

answer.text: 1, then 2, then 3, then 4

feedback.text: Building and demoing before discussing and distilling reverses the cycle.

answer.text: 3, then 1, then 4, then 2

feedback.text: The acceptance tests (4, Distill) must be written before development (1, Develop).

generalfeedback.text: Mapping the activities to stages: (3) is Discuss, (4) is Distill, (1) is Develop, and (2) is Demo. The correct order therefore is 3, 4, 1, 2 — Discuss, Distill, Develop, Demo.

name.text: What "done" means at the acceptance level

questiontext.text: In ATDD, when is a feature considered "done" at the acceptance level?

answer.text: When it satisfies the agreed acceptance criteria — the acceptance tests pass and stakeholders confirm it in the Demo

feedback.text: Correct — "done" is defined by the agreed acceptance criteria being met and verified.

answer.text: When the developer feels the code is finished, regardless of the criteria

feedback.text: "Done" is defined by the agreed acceptance criteria, not by individual feeling.

answer.text: When 100% branch coverage is reached, whatever the behaviour

feedback.text: Coverage is a separate metric; acceptance "done" is meeting the agreed criteria.

answer.text: When the code compiles without warnings

feedback.text: Compiling cleanly is not the same as satisfying the customer's acceptance criteria.

generalfeedback.text: ATDD makes "done" objective and shared: the feature is done when it meets the acceptance criteria agreed up front — the acceptance tests pass and the stakeholders confirm it in the Demo. This removes ambiguity about whether the right thing was actually delivered.

questiontext.text: The four stages of the ATDD cycle occur in the order Discuss, Distill, Develop, Demo.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — that is the order: understand, capture as tests, build, then verify with stakeholders.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: The order is exactly Discuss, Distill, Develop, Demo.

generalfeedback.text: The ATDD cycle runs Discuss (understand the requirement with examples), Distill (turn examples into acceptance tests), Develop (implement, making the tests pass with unit TDD inside), and Demo (verify the result with stakeholders).

name.text: Place activity: exploring a story with examples

questiontext.text: The business owner, a developer, and a tester sit together and talk through a new user story, raising "what should happen if...?" examples to reach a shared understanding before anything is written down as a test. Which ATDD stage is this?

answer.text: Discuss

feedback.text: Correct — exploring the requirement with stakeholders through examples is the Discuss stage.

answer.text: Distill

feedback.text: Distill is when those examples are written up as acceptance tests; the conversation itself is Discuss.

answer.text: Develop

feedback.text: Develop is implementation; the up-front conversation with examples is Discuss.

answer.text: Demo

feedback.text: Demo verifies the finished feature; the initial exploration of the story is Discuss.

generalfeedback.text: This is Discuss: the Three Amigos explore the story together, using concrete "what if" examples to build a shared understanding of the requirement. Turning those examples into written acceptance tests would be the next stage, Distill.
